title: A channel flow is checked by what must be conserved or known in closed form: the same flux through every arm, and a parabola raised by a wall-slip term
summary: A colour map of speed in a stepped microchannel and a profile plot of slip flow against no-slip flow at a Knudsen number of 0.05. The first is read through mass conservation and the no-slip wall, the second through the closed-form slip-flow profile and its mean-velocity enhancement.

media.alt: Velocity profile across a channel from y = 0 to 20 micrometres, with speed on the horizontal axis from 0 to 0.3 millimetres per second. A dashed black parabola starts at zero speed at both walls and peaks at 0.25. A solid black curve, with a red dotted numerical curve lying exactly on it, starts at 0.05 at both walls and peaks at 0.30. The title gives Kn = 0.05 and an enhancement of 1.3 times the mean velocity.

source.caption: Slip flow at Kn = 0.05: analytic and numerical profile compared with no-slip Poiseuille
group: 13_mf_slip_flow: Slip flow at Kn = 0.05, analytic and numerical profile compared with no-slip Poiseuille (representative)
12_mf_micromixer_demo: Stokes flow in a stepped microchannel from the geometry gallery, velocity magnitude
source.note: The page teaches how to read a Stokes-flow speed map and a first-order slip-flow profile with standard theory (Poiseuille flow, Maxwell slip). Numbers quoted are printed on the figures, read from them, or computed in the Apply script. The micromixer demo also has a cfdcore counterpart covered by the design-study explainer.

read_the_figure.question: Does the computed flow behave as Stokes flow must (no-slip walls, the same flux through every arm of a constant-width channel), and how much does a first-order wall-slip condition change the profile and the mean speed at a given Knudsen number?
read_the_figure.axes: Stepped channel: x and y are position in micrometres (0 to 260 and 0 to 180); colour is speed magnitude in mm/s from about 0 to 2.8; the white region is outside the channel. Slip flow: y is position across the gap from 0 to 20 micrometres, x is speed in mm/s from 0 to 0.3; dashed is no-slip Poiseuille, solid is the analytic slip solution, red dotted is a numerical solution of the boundary-value problem.
look_at: Stepped channel: the channel is 20 micrometres wide in every arm; the speed is highest along the centre line of each arm and falls to near zero at the walls.
Stepped channel: the maximum colour, about 2.8 mm/s, is the same in the horizontal and vertical arms, as a constant flux through constant width requires.
Stepped channel: in each horizontal arm the row of cells next to the lower wall is dark while the row next to the upper wall is blue (about 1 mm/s); the arm is not symmetric about its centre line.
Stepped channel: the title is cut off by the colour bar; the visible end of the mass-conservation residual is of order 1e-11.
Slip flow: both solid curves start at 0.05 mm/s on the walls, not at zero; the red dotted curve cannot be distinguished from the solid curve.
Slip flow: the peak is 0.30 mm/s against 0.25 for no-slip.
read_the_figure.proves: The stepped-channel map shows that the geometry, boundary tagging and mesh give a smooth channel flow with the right qualitative structure, and a printed mass-conservation residual of order 1e-11. The slip figure shows that the numerical solution reproduces the analytic slip profile, and that the profile has a wall slip of 0.05 mm/s and a peak 20 percent higher than no-slip, a mean 1.3 times higher.
if_wrong: Different peak speeds in the arms of a constant-width channel: a leak, a mesh problem or a wrong outlet condition.
Non-zero speed at a no-slip wall in the colour map: plotting resampling error, not physics, if it is only on one side.
A numerical curve that departs from the analytic one near the wall: the slip condition is applied with the wrong sign, coefficient or direction.
A slip enhancement far from 1 + 6 Kn at small Kn: the slip length is mis-scaled.
must_check: The map is resampled onto a pixel grid in a way that is symmetric about the channel; a one-sided offset is a plotting artefact.
Mass flux through two cross-sections is compared, not just the maximum colour.
A Knudsen number is stated with the length it is based on, and its regime of validity is named.
Slip coefficient, accommodation and the gap are stated so the analytic curve can be reproduced.
Titles and colour bars do not overlap, so printed numbers can be read.
as_drawn: Stepped channel: arms 20 micrometres wide; horizontal arms span x of 0 to 100, 80 to 180 and 160 to 260; vertical arms at x of 80 to 100 and 160 to 180; speed maximum about 2.8 mm/s; coarse square cells of a few micrometres. Title lists three boundary tags and a mass-conservation residual cut off at '.43e-11'.
Slip flow: gap from 0 to 20 micrometres; no-slip peak 0.25 mm/s; slip curve 0.05 mm/s at both walls and 0.30 mm/s at the centre; title Kn = 0.05, enhancement 1.3 times mean velocity.

terms.meaning: Flow at very low Reynolds number in which inertia is negligible and viscous forces balance pressure, so the flow is smooth and reversible.
The fluid velocity at a solid wall equals the wall velocity, here zero.
For incompressible flow the volume flux through any cross-section of a channel is the same; in a constant-width channel the peak speed is therefore the same in every arm.
The ratio of the molecular mean free path to a flow length, here the gap; it measures how far the fluid departs from a continuum.
The regime, at Knudsen numbers of roughly 0.001 to 0.1, in which the continuum equations still hold in the bulk but the wall velocity is not zero.
The wall velocity is proportional to the velocity gradient at the wall, with the mean free path as the proportionality constant at full accommodation.
A label attached to parts of the mesh boundary (inlet, outlet, wall) so that conditions can be applied to them.

remember: In Stokes flow in a constant-width channel the peak speed is the same in every arm.
A parabola has mean speed two thirds of its peak.
First-order slip adds a constant to the Poiseuille profile; it does not change the curvature.
The mean-speed enhancement is 1 plus 6 Kn in a plane channel with full accommodation.
A one-sided asymmetry in a symmetric channel's map is a plotting or sampling suspect.

understand.title: What the colour map is evidence of
understand.text: A map of speed shows that the mesh, the tagged boundaries and the solver produce a smooth flow that follows the channel: speed is zero at the walls, largest on the centre lines and nearly equal in all arms. The printed residual of order 1e-11 says the discrete solution conserves mass to rounding level. It does not test the pressure drop or the corners, where Stokes flow is smooth but the mesh matters.

understand.title: The asymmetry between the walls
understand.text: In the horizontal arms, the cells next to the lower wall are dark, as for a no-slip wall, but the cells next to the upper wall have a speed of about 1 mm/s. A channel symmetric about its centre line should have the same speed next to both walls. The most likely cause is that the field is sampled at cell centres or on a raster that does not reach the upper wall, but the figure does not say.

understand.title: What slip adds
understand.text: With the wall velocity proportional to the wall shear, the parabola is lifted by a constant. For a gap H and no-slip peak u0 the wall shear is 4 u0 over H on each wall, so the slip is 4 Kn u0 if the mean free path is Kn times H. The figure's 0.05 mm/s follows from Kn = 0.05 and u0 = 0.25 mm/s. The curvature of the profile is unchanged, so the solid curve is the dashed one translated right by 0.05 mm/s.

understand.title: The enhancement of the mean
understand.text: The mean of the no-slip profile is two thirds of its peak. Adding the slip 4 Kn u0 changes the mean by a factor of 1 plus 6 Kn, which is 1.3 for Kn = 0.05, as printed. The result relies on first-order slip with unit accommodation; at Knudsen numbers near 0.1 second-order terms and Knudsen layers matter.

steps.title: Mass conservation in a constant-width channel
steps.note: For a parabolic profile in every arm. With u_max = 2.8 mm/s and W = 20 micrometres, Q is about 3.7e-8 m^2/s per unit depth.

steps.title: Reynolds number check
steps.note: With a water-like fluid (assumed) and mean speed about 1.9 mm/s, Re is about 0.04, so inertia is negligible and Stokes flow is justified.

steps.title: No-slip Poiseuille profile
steps.note: Gap H = 20 micrometres; the dashed curve with peak 0.25 mm/s.

steps.title: Maxwell slip at the wall
steps.note: With Kn = lambda/H and full accommodation (assumed). For Kn = 0.05 and 0.25 mm/s this gives 0.05 mm/s.

steps.title: Slip profile
steps.note: A constant shift; the peak is 0.30 mm/s.

steps.title: Mean enhancement
steps.note: For Kn = 0.05 this is 1.3, the printed enhancement.

worked.title: Reproduce the slip numbers from Kn and the no-slip peak
worked.problem: The no-slip peak is 0.25 mm/s in a 20 micrometre gap and Kn = 0.05. With first-order Maxwell slip at full accommodation, find the wall slip, the slip peak and the mean enhancement, and compare with the figure.
worked.answer: 0.05 mm/s at the wall, 0.30 mm/s at the centre and a factor of 1.3 on the mean: all three equal the figure. The full-accommodation assumption is thus consistent with the drawing, although the figure does not state it.

analyze.q: In the stepped channel the cells next to the upper wall of a horizontal arm show about 1 mm/s while those next to the lower wall are dark. List two plotting causes and one check on the raw data that would distinguish them.
analyze.hint: Cell-centre sampling versus node values; compare the speed profile across an arm.

analyze.q: The channel has the same width in every arm. How does the colour bar maximum, the same in horizontal and vertical arms, follow from mass conservation, and what would a different maximum in one arm mean?
analyze.hint: Q is the same; the width is the same.

analyze.q: For Kn = 0.1, what does the first-order formula give for the enhancement, and which neglected effects start to matter there?
analyze.hint: 1 + 6 Kn; second-order slip and Knudsen layers.

evaluate.q: The demo is called a micromixer in the project text, but the figure shows a single channel with one fluid. What does the figure demonstrate, and what claim should it not support?
The numerical profile overlays the analytic one so tightly that the dotted line is invisible. Is that a sufficient presentation of the agreement?
evaluate.hint: Where would a residual plot help?

create: Design a figure that shows the stepped channel's flux through five cross-sections as a bar chart with the printed mass-conservation residual, so the conservation claim can be seen and not only stated.
Extend the slip figure to three Knudsen numbers (for example 0.01, 0.05 and 0.1) and state which curve you would not trust with first-order slip and why.

checks.q: Why must the peak speed be the same in every arm of a constant-width channel?
checks.hint: What is the same in every cross-section?
checks.answer: The volume flux is the same and the profile shape is the same, so the peak is the same.

checks.q: A parabolic profile has peak 2.8 mm/s in a 20 micrometre channel. What is the flux per unit depth?
checks.hint: Two thirds times peak times width.

checks.q: Why does slip raise the mean speed by 1 + 6 Kn in a plane channel?
checks.hint: Compare the shift with the mean of the parabola.
checks.answer: The slip shift is 4 Kn u0, the no-slip mean is 2/3 u0, so the ratio of the shift to the mean is 6 Kn.

checks.q: A slip figure shows an overlay of numerical and analytic curves. What additional evidence would you want?
checks.answer: The residual of the two curves, a mesh refinement showing it falls, and the slip coefficient and accommodation used.

checks.q: What test would show the channel map conserves mass through the corners?
checks.hint: Compute the same quantity at several sections.
checks.answer: Integrate the speed across several cross-sections in the horizontal and vertical arms, including near the corners, and report the relative difference between them.

provenance.notes: Disclosure: the micromixer map title lists internal boundary tags (inlet, outlet, wall) and a 'Geometry gallery' module name, and the project description says the case runs through 'the solver's own geometry and meshing pipeline'; none repeated. No PLACEHOLDER footer, thesis remark or solver name seen in these two. Owner review: (1) the micromixer map's title is cut off by the colour bar. (2) The map is called a micromixer in the project text but shows a single stepped channel with one speed field and no species, so it demonstrates geometry, tagging and Stokes flow, not mixing. (3) In each horizontal arm the cells beside the upper wall show about 1 mm/s while those beside the lower wall are near zero, an asymmetry that looks like a sampling artefact. (4) The slip figure does not state the slip coefficient or accommodation; the printed numbers are reproduced with first-order slip at full accommodation. (5) The slip curves overlay so closely that the numerical curve is invisible; a residual would show agreement.
